evidence_grades.A: Original archival document, manuscript, map, photograph or physical record directly inspected.
evidence_grades.B: Contemporary published primary source directly inspected.
evidence_grades.C: Archival catalogue, finding aid, published abstract or transcription; underlying original not inspected.
evidence_grades.D: Secondary historical interpretation or modern report.
evidence_grades.E: Unverified lead, inference or candidate source not adequately checked.

claims.claim: Clontarf sheds existed at the water's edge and were formerly used for fish curing.
A cluster of herring sheds fronted the Coast Road and the route later associated with Vernon Avenue extended north from it.
An 1836 OS Name Book described a road through the Sheds to the shore.
Patrick Toole held property in the Sheds and a dwellinghouse in the Green of the Sheds.
A 1728 harbour map labels a Clontarf coastal feature Herring Sheds.
A print titled The Sheds of Clontarfe was made in 1785 by Thomas Malton after Francis Wheatley.
A 1744–1745 Giles King view contains a numbered key identifying the Sheds of Clontarf.
Herringtowne was a name for the Sheds or fishing port in 1693.
Christmas Weekes wrote from Clontarf in 1786 about works supplying shipping with water.
A 1704 John Greene Junior survey of Donnycarney covers lands in the Parish of Clontarf.
